1.summary: On the plains of Moab in the fortieth year, Moses begins his farewell by recalling the leaders appointed at Horeb and Israel's refusal to enter the land at Kadesh Barnea.
1.lookfor: Notice how Moses speaks to his hearers as if they had been there themselves, his charge to the judges, and the picture of God carrying Israel like a son.

names.name: Arabah
names.gloss: The deep rift valley of the Jordan, running south through the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba.

names.name: Horeb
names.gloss: Deuteronomy's usual name for Mount Sinai, where the covenant was given.

names.name: Kadesh Barnea
names.gloss: The oasis on the southern edge of Canaan from which the spies were sent.

names.name: Mount Seir
names.gloss: The mountains of Edom, southeast of the Dead Sea.

names.name: Anakim
names.gloss: A clan of unusually tall people living in Canaan, whose size terrified the spies.

names.name: Caleb
names.gloss: One of the twelve spies, who urged Israel to trust God and take the land.

insights.title: Devarim: words
insights.body: The book opens, "These are the words which Moses spoke" (1:1), and its Hebrew name is Devarim, "words." The English name comes from the Greek Deuteronomion, "second law," based on the phrase "a copy of this law" in the law about kings. It is less a new law than Moses' preaching of the old one to a new generation.

insights.title: Eleven days, forty years
insights.body: "It is eleven days' journey from Horeb" to Kadesh Barnea (1:2), yet Moses speaks "in the fortieth year" (1:3). The two verses set side by side tell the whole sad story of Numbers. The delay was not distance but unbelief.

insights.title: Speaking to a new generation
insights.body: Almost everyone who stood at Horeb has died, yet Moses keeps saying "you": you came near, you murmured in your tents (1:22, 1:27). He treats the new generation as sharing their parents' story. Later he says the covenant was made "with us, even us, who are all of us here alive today."

insights.title: Sharing the load
insights.body: Moses recalls, "I am not able to bear you myself alone" (1:9), and appoints leaders over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens (1:15). Exodus tells how the idea came from his father-in-law Jethro; here Moses tells it as his own proposal agreed by the people. Both versions stress wise, well-known leaders chosen from the tribes.

insights.title: The judgment is God's
insights.body: Judges must "hear the small and the great alike" and not be afraid of anyone, "for the judgment is God's" (1:17). They must also judge fairly for the foreigner (1:16). King Jehoshaphat later repeats the charge to his judges.

insights.title: Whose idea were the spies?
insights.body: Here the people propose sending spies, and Moses agrees (1:22-23). Numbers says God told Moses to send them. Read together, God grants the people's request; the sin lies in refusing to go up after the report.

insights.title: Carried like a son
insights.body: Moses reminds them how Yahweh "bore you, as a man does bear his son" all the way through the wilderness (1:31). The people, though, said Yahweh brought them out "because Yahweh hated us" (1:27). The same events were read as love by Moses and as hatred by a frightened people.

insights.title: Too late to obey
insights.body: After refusing, the people decided to go up anyway and were chased "as bees do" (1:44). How can you tell the difference between real repentance and trying to undo consequences on your own terms?

2.summary: Israel circles the hills of Seir, passes Edom, Moab and Ammon without fighting because God has given them their lands, and then defeats Sihon king of Heshbon.
2.lookfor: Notice the nations Israel must leave alone and why, the short notes about ancient peoples, and the turn when Israel is told to fight Sihon.

names.name: Esau
names.gloss: Jacob's twin brother, ancestor of the Edomites.

names.name: Ar
names.gloss: A city or district of Moab near the Arnon.

names.name: Emim
names.gloss: An ancient tall people who once lived in Moab.

names.name: Rephaim
names.gloss: A name for legendary giant peoples of the region before Israel.

names.name: Zamzummim
names.gloss: The Ammonites' name for the Rephaim who once lived in their land.

names.name: Caphtorim
names.gloss: People from Caphtor, probably Crete, linked with the Philistines.

names.name: Sihon
names.gloss: The Amorite king who ruled from Heshbon, east of the Jordan.

names.name: Zered
names.gloss: A brook running into the south end of the Dead Sea, the border of Moab.

insights.title: God gives land to others too
insights.body: God tells Israel not to take "so much as for the sole of the foot" from Edom, "because I have given Mount Seir to Esau" (2:5), and says the same of Moab and Ammon (2:9, 2:19). Yahweh is not only Israel's local god; he allots lands to other nations. Amos later makes the same point about the Philistines and Arameans.

insights.title: Notes on ancient peoples
insights.body: Brackets in the text pause the speech to explain who lived in these lands before: the Emim, the Horites, the Zamzummim, the Avvim (2:10-12, 2:20-23). The name Rephaim also appears in texts from the ancient city of Ugarit, where it refers to the honoured dead. Israel's own conquest is set alongside other peoples' displacements.

insights.title: You have lacked nothing
insights.body: "These forty years, Yahweh your God has been with you. You have lacked nothing" (2:7). The wilderness years were a judgment, yet God provided throughout. Nehemiah's prayer repeats the claim.

insights.title: Thirty-eight years
insights.body: From Kadesh Barnea to the brook Zered took "thirty-eight years" (2:14), until all the fighting men of the first generation had died. Only then does God say, "Rise up" (2:24). The march to the land resumes when the sentence of Numbers 14 is complete.

insights.title: A hardened spirit
insights.body: Israel offers Sihon peaceful passage and to pay for food and water (2:26-29). He refuses, because "Yahweh your God hardened his spirit" (2:30). As with Pharaoh, the text holds both Sihon's choice and God's purpose together without explaining how.

insights.title: Cherem: devoted to destruction
insights.body: Israel "utterly destroyed every inhabited city, with the women and the little ones" (2:34). The verb comes from cherem, something devoted to God by being destroyed. It is among the hardest ideas in Scripture, and scholars debate how far such accounts use the stock language of ancient war reports; the text itself presents it as judgment.

insights.title: Leaving others alone
insights.body: Israel had to march past fertile land God had given to others. What would it mean for you to respect what God has given someone else, even when you could take it?

3.summary: Israel defeats Og king of Bashan, the land east of the Jordan is given to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh, and Moses' plea to enter the land is refused as Joshua is named to lead.
3.lookfor: Notice the size of Og's bed, the arrangement with the eastern tribes, and the conversation between Moses and God at the end.

names.name: Og
names.gloss: King of Bashan, remembered as the last of the Rephaim.

names.name: Bashan
names.gloss: A fertile plateau east of the Sea of Galilee, today the Golan and southern Syria.

names.name: Argob
names.gloss: A district of Bashan with sixty fortified cities.

names.name: Hermon
names.gloss: The tall snow-capped mountain at the northern edge of the land.

names.name: Rabbah
names.gloss: The Ammonite capital, today Amman in Jordan.

names.name: Pisgah
names.gloss: A ridge in Moab overlooking the Jordan valley and the land beyond.

names.name: Beth Peor
names.gloss: A place in Moab near where Israel camped; Moses is later buried in the valley there.

insights.title: Og's iron bed
insights.body: Og's "bedstead of iron" was nine cubits long, about four metres (3:11). Some scholars think it was a coffin of black basalt, which looks like iron; the region of Bashan is dotted with large ancient stone dolmen tombs. The bracketed note says it could still be seen in Rabbah.

insights.title: One mountain, three names
insights.body: "The Sidonians call Hermon Sirion, and the Amorites call it Senir" (3:9). Sirion also appears as Hermon's name in texts from Ugarit. Little asides like this treat the land as a real place known to many peoples.

insights.title: The eastern tribes' promise
insights.body: Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh receive land east of the Jordan, but their fighting men must cross and fight "until Yahweh gives rest to your brothers" (3:18-20). The deal is told at length in Numbers 32, and Joshua holds them to it.

insights.title: Angry with me for your sakes
insights.body: Moses begs to "go over and see the good land" (3:25), but God refuses: "Let this satisfy you. Speak no more to me of this matter" (3:26). Numbers ties Moses' exclusion to striking the rock; Deuteronomy says God was angry with Moses "for your sakes," bound up with the people's failures.

insights.title: What god is like you?
insights.body: Moses' prayer begins with praise: "For what god is there in heaven or in earth that can do works like yours?" (3:24). It echoes the Song of the Sea. Even a prayer that will be refused begins with who God is.

insights.title: Encourage Joshua
insights.body: Instead of entering, Moses must "commission Joshua, and encourage him, and strengthen him" (3:28). His last task is to prepare someone else. The book of Joshua opens with God repeating the charge: "Be strong and courageous."

insights.title: A prayer answered no
insights.body: Moses, who prayed Israel out of disaster many times, hears no to his own request. Paul too asked three times for relief and was told God's grace was enough. How do you live with a prayer God has said no to?

4.summary: Moses urges Israel to keep God's law as their wisdom, never to make images since they saw no form at Horeb, and warns of exile while promising that those who seek God there will find him.
4.lookfor: Notice the repeated call to remember what their eyes saw, the reasons given against images, and the hope offered beyond exile.

names.name: Baal Peor
names.gloss: The place in Moab where Israel worshipped the local Baal and suffered a plague.

names.name: Horeb
names.gloss: Mount Sinai, where God spoke from the fire.

names.name: Bezer
names.gloss: A city of refuge in Reuben's territory.

names.name: Golan
names.gloss: A city of refuge in Bashan, giving its name to today's Golan Heights.

insights.title: Don't add or take away
insights.body: "You shall not add to the word which I command you, neither shall you take away from it" (4:2). The same warning returns later in Deuteronomy, and Revelation closes with a similar one. Ancient treaties and law collections sometimes ended with curses on anyone who altered them.

insights.title: Wisdom in the sight of the nations
insights.body: Keeping the law will make the nations say, "Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people" (4:6). Israel's obedience was meant to be a public witness. Two questions follow: what nation has a god so near, and laws so righteous (4:7-8)?

insights.title: A voice, but no form
insights.body: "You heard the voice of words, but you saw no form; you only heard a voice" (4:12). Because God revealed himself by speaking, not by a shape, Israel must not make an image of him in any form (4:15-18). God is known by his word.

insights.title: Heaven and earth as witnesses
insights.body: "I call heaven and earth to witness against you today" (4:26). Ancient treaties listed gods as witnesses to the agreement. Deuteronomy, which allows no other gods, calls on heaven and earth instead, as it does again in chapters 30 and 32.

insights.title: Seek and you will find
insights.body: Even in exile, "you shall seek Yahweh your God, and you shall find him, when you search after him with all your heart" (4:29). Jeremiah sends the same promise to the exiles in Babylon. The warning of exile comes with a door left open.

insights.title: The iron furnace
insights.body: Egypt is "the iron furnace" (4:20), the furnace used to smelt metal. Slavery was a place of intense heat and pressure, from which God took Israel to be "a people of inheritance." Solomon and Jeremiah reuse the image.

insights.title: No one else
insights.body: "Yahweh is God. There is no one else besides him" (4:35), and again, "There is no one else" (4:39). These are among the clearest statements of one God in the Torah. Isaiah repeats the words, and Hebrews quotes the warning that God is "a devouring fire" (4:24).

insights.title: Lest you forget
insights.body: Moses tells Israel to keep their soul diligently "lest you forget the things which your eyes saw" (4:9) and to teach them to their grandchildren. What has God done in your life that you are in danger of forgetting?

5.summary: Moses repeats the Ten Commandments given at Horeb and recalls how the terrified people asked him to stand between them and God.
5.lookfor: Compare the commandments with Exodus 20, especially the Sabbath and coveting, and notice what the people ask of Moses and what God says in reply.

names.name: Horeb
names.gloss: Mount Sinai, where God spoke the commandments from the fire.

insights.title: With us, alive today
insights.body: "Yahweh didn't make this covenant with our fathers, but with us, even us, who are all of us here alive today" (5:3). Most of the hearers were children or not yet born at Horeb. Each generation is to hear the commandments as spoken to them.

insights.title: A different reason for the Sabbath
insights.body: In Exodus the Sabbath recalls God resting after creation. Here Israel must remember they were slaves in Egypt (5:15), and the rest is given so "that your male servant and your female servant may rest as well as you" (5:14). The day of rest is also a day of justice for workers.

insights.title: Wife first
insights.body: Exodus says first not to covet a neighbour's house, then his wife. Deuteronomy puts the wife first, uses a separate verb for desiring the house, and adds his field (5:21). The small changes suggest a settled people with fields to protect.

insights.title: Counting to ten
insights.body: Traditions number the commandments differently. Jewish tradition counts "I am Yahweh your God" (5:6) as the first word; Catholics and Lutherans join the ban on other gods and images and split coveting in two; Orthodox and Reformed Christians count the images command separately. The text itself calls them ten words without numbering them.

insights.title: Ratsach: murder
insights.body: "You shall not murder" (5:17) uses ratsach, a word for unlawful killing, the same root used for the manslayer in the cities of refuge. It is narrower than the general word for killing. Jesus traces the commandment back to anger in the heart.

insights.title: Standing between
insights.body: "I stood between Yahweh and you at that time" (5:5). The people beg Moses to go near and listen for them (5:27), and God approves (5:28). Hebrews contrasts that terrifying mountain with the way believers now come near through Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant.

insights.title: Oh that there were such a heart
insights.body: God says, "Oh that there were such a heart in them, that they would fear me, and keep all my commandments always" (5:29). It sounds like longing. What would it look like for God's commands to come from the heart rather than from fear alone?

6.summary: Moses gives the Shema, the call to love Yahweh with all your heart, soul and might, and tells Israel to keep his words before them always and teach them to their children.
6.lookfor: Notice the opening confession, the three "all"s, the places where God's words are to be kept, and the warning about forgetting God in prosperity.

names.name: Massah
names.gloss: A place in the wilderness whose name means "testing," where Israel demanded water.

insights.title: Shema: hear
insights.body: "Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one" (6:4). Shema, "hear," also means to obey. The Hebrew can be translated several ways, including Yahweh our God, Yahweh alone; either way it claims Israel's undivided loyalty. Jews recite it morning and evening, and it is traditionally the last words on the lips of the dying.

insights.title: The greatest commandment
insights.body: Asked which commandment is first, Jesus quotes this passage, adding "mind" to heart, soul and strength, and pairs it with loving your neighbour. A scribe agrees that this is more than all burnt offerings.

insights.title: With all your might
insights.body: The third "all" is me'od (6:5), normally an adverb meaning "very" or "much," here used as a noun: your "muchness." Rabbinic interpreters took it to include one's wealth. Heart, soul and might together leave no part of life out.

insights.title: On hand, forehead and door
insights.body: God's words are to be bound on the hand, between the eyes, and written on doorposts (6:8-9). Jewish practice fulfils this with tefillin, small boxes holding these verses, some found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and the mezuzah fixed to the doorpost. Jesus criticised those who made their phylacteries broad for show.

insights.title: When your son asks
insights.body: "When your son asks you... what do the testimonies... mean?" (6:20), the answer is a story: "We were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt" (6:21). The Passover Haggadah gives this question to the wise son of its famous four sons. Faith is passed on by telling what God did.

insights.title: Jesus in the wilderness
insights.body: When tempted, Jesus answers from this chapter: "You shall not tempt Yahweh your God" (6:16) and "You shall fear Yahweh your God; and you shall serve him" (6:13). Where Israel failed its test in the wilderness, Jesus stands firm in his.

insights.title: Cities you didn't build
insights.body: Israel will receive cities, houses, wells and vineyards "which you didn't build... which you didn't plant" (6:10-11). The danger is that full stomachs forget the giver (6:12). Joshua's farewell repeats the list as pure gift.

insights.title: When you sit and when you walk
insights.body: God's words are to be talked about at home, on the road, at bedtime and on waking (6:7). Where in your ordinary day could his words find a place?

7.summary: Israel is to destroy the nations of Canaan and their worship and not intermarry with them, for God chose Israel out of love, not because they were many.
7.lookfor: Notice the reasons given for the harsh commands, why God chose Israel, and the promise that the conquest will happen little by little.

names.name: Girgashite
names.gloss: One of the seven peoples of Canaan, otherwise little known.

names.name: Perizzite
names.gloss: A people of Canaan, possibly villagers living in unwalled settlements.

names.name: Hivite
names.gloss: A people of central and northern Canaan, including the Gibeonites.

names.name: Jebusite
names.gloss: The people who held Jerusalem until David captured it.

insights.title: A hard command
insights.body: Israel must "utterly destroy" the seven nations, make no covenant and show no mercy (7:2). The reason given is religious: "he will turn away your son from following me" (7:4). Readers have long struggled with this; scholars point out that the same chapter forbids intermarriage, implying the peoples remain, and that Joshua and Judges show many Canaanites living on.

insights.title: Not because you were many
insights.body: "Yahweh didn't set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples" (7:7). The only reason given is that Yahweh loves them and keeps his oath (7:8). Election is grace, not reward.

insights.title: Segullah: treasured possession
insights.body: Israel is "a people for his own possession" (7:6), in Hebrew segullah, a king's personal treasure. Peter applies the language to the church, "a people for God's own possession."

insights.title: Asherah poles
insights.body: Israel must cut down the Canaanites' "Asherah poles" (7:5), wooden cult objects linked with the goddess Asherah. Inscriptions found at Kuntillet Ajrud in the Sinai, from around 800 BC, mention Yahweh together with his Asherah, showing that some Israelites later blended her worship with Yahweh's.

insights.title: A thousand generations
insights.body: Yahweh is "the faithful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness... to a thousand generations" (7:9). Paul uses the same title: "God is faithful." The contrast with punishment that reaches only to the third and fourth generation shows which side God leans toward.

insights.title: The hornet and little by little
insights.body: God will send "the hornet" (7:20), which interpreters take literally, as a picture of panic, or as a symbol of Egyptian power in Canaan. He will also drive the nations out "little by little" (7:22), so the land does not fall to wild animals. Exodus gives the same two promises.

insights.title: Chosen for love
insights.body: Israel was chosen not for size or strength but because God loved them. How does it change you to know God's love was not earned?

8.summary: Moses calls Israel to remember how God humbled and fed them in the wilderness, and warns that in the rich land ahead they must not forget him or think their own power made them wealthy.
8.lookfor: Notice why God led them through hunger, the description of the good land, and the danger that comes with being full.

insights.title: Not by bread only
insights.body: God fed Israel with manna "that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of Yahweh's mouth" (8:3). Jesus answers the devil with this verse after forty days of fasting in the wilderness.

insights.title: Why the hard years?
insights.body: God led them through the wilderness "that he might humble you, to prove you, to know what was in your heart" (8:2), and disciplined them "as a man disciplines his son" (8:5). Hebrews and Proverbs take up the same picture of hardship as a father's training.

insights.title: Clothes that didn't wear out
insights.body: "Your clothing didn't grow old on you, neither did your foot swell, these forty years" (8:4). The quiet miracles of daily provision are easy to overlook. Nehemiah's prayer remembers this too.

insights.title: The seven species
insights.body: The land is one of "wheat and barley, and vines and fig trees and pomegranates; a land of olive trees and honey" (8:8). Jewish tradition calls these the seven species; the honey is usually understood as date syrup. They were the produce brought as first fruits to the Temple.

insights.title: Grace after meals
insights.body: "You shall eat and be full, and you shall bless Yahweh your God for the good land" (8:10). This verse is the basis of the Jewish grace after meals, said after eating rather than only before. Thanks are due when the hunger is already gone.

insights.title: My power and my hand
insights.body: The danger of plenty is to say, "My power and the might of my hand has gotten me this wealth" (8:17). Moses answers, "it is he who gives you power to get wealth" (8:18). Jesus' parable of the rich fool shows the same forgetfulness.

insights.title: Full and forgetful
insights.body: Moses fears prosperity more than the wilderness. In your life, does comfort make it easier or harder to remember God?

9.summary: Moses warns Israel that they will not win the land because of their righteousness, and retells the golden calf and his forty days of prayer for them.
9.lookfor: Notice the list of Israel's failures, what Moses did with the tablets and the calf, and the arguments he used when he prayed.

names.name: Anakim
names.gloss: The tall clan whose reputation frightened the spies.

names.name: Taberah
names.gloss: A camp where fire broke out because of the people's complaining.

names.name: Kibroth Hattaavah
names.gloss: "Graves of craving," where Israel complained for meat.

insights.title: Not for your righteousness
insights.body: Moses says three times that Israel will not take the land because of their righteousness (9:4-6). The reasons are the wickedness of the nations and God's promise to the patriarchs (9:5). Genesis had said the Amorites' iniquity was not yet complete in Abraham's day.

insights.title: Stiff-necked
insights.body: Israel is "a stiff-necked people" (9:6, 9:13), like an ox that will not bend its neck to the yoke. Stephen uses the same word for his hearers in Acts.

insights.title: Written by God's finger
insights.body: The tablets were "written with God's finger" (9:10). Jesus says he casts out demons "by God's finger," a phrase echoing Egypt's magicians as well as these tablets.

insights.title: He prayed for Aaron too
insights.body: "Yahweh was angry enough with Aaron to destroy him. I prayed for Aaron also" (9:20). Exodus does not mention this. Aaron, who made the calf, owed his life to his brother's prayer.

insights.title: Dust in the brook
insights.body: Moses burned the calf, ground it "as fine as dust," and threw it into the brook from the mountain (9:21). Exodus adds that he made the people drink it. The idol was reduced to nothing and washed away.

insights.title: Praying with God's reputation
insights.body: Moses argues that the nations would say Yahweh "was not able to bring them into the land" (9:28), and that Israel is God's own people and inheritance (9:29). He appeals to God's name and promises, not Israel's merit, as he does again after the spies.

insights.title: Remember, and don't forget
insights.body: "Remember, and don't forget, how you provoked Yahweh" (9:7). Why might remembering past failures be good for a community, not just shameful?

10.summary: Moses tells of the second set of tablets placed in the ark and the setting apart of Levi, then sums up what God requires: to fear, love and serve him, and to love the foreigner.
10.lookfor: Notice the travel note dropped into the speech, the great question of what God requires, and how God's character shapes Israel's conduct.

names.name: Moserah
names.gloss: A desert camp where, according to this verse, Aaron died.

names.name: Eleazar
names.gloss: Aaron's son, who became high priest after him.

names.name: Jotbathah
names.gloss: A desert stopping place described as a land of streams.

insights.title: Tablets in the ark
insights.body: The new tablets are put in an ark of acacia wood (10:5). Ancient treaties were often deposited in a sanctuary before the gods who witnessed them. Israel's covenant documents rest beneath the place where God meets his people.

insights.title: A travel note
insights.body: A bracketed note interrupts Moses' speech with stopping places and Aaron's death "at Moserah" (10:6). Numbers places Aaron's death on Mount Hor; Moserah may be the district in which the mountain stood. The note explains why Levi was set apart "at that time" (10:8).

insights.title: What does Yahweh require?
insights.body: "What does Yahweh your God require of you, but to fear Yahweh your God, to walk in all his ways, and to love him, and to serve" him (10:12). Micah later asks the same question and answers: to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly with God.

insights.title: Circumcise the heart
insights.body: "Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart" (10:16). The outward sign of the covenant must be matched inwardly. Deuteronomy later promises that God himself will do it, and Paul takes up the image.

insights.title: A God who takes no bribe
insights.body: Yahweh is "God of gods, and Lord of lords... who doesn't respect persons, nor takes reward" (10:17). The mightiest title in the chapter leads straight into justice for orphans and widows (10:18). Peter learns that God shows no favouritism.

insights.title: Love the foreigner
insights.body: God "loves the foreigner," so Israel must too, "for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt" (10:18-19). Israel's own past becomes the reason for compassion. Leviticus gives the same command.

insights.title: Seventy to the stars
insights.body: "Your fathers went down into Egypt with seventy persons; and now... as the stars of the sky" (10:22). Genesis counts the seventy, and God's promise to Abraham used the stars.

insights.title: Because you were once
insights.body: Israel was to treat foreigners well because they had been foreigners. What part of your own story could make you more compassionate to others?

11.summary: Moses urges Israel to love and obey God, contrasts Egypt's irrigated fields with a land that depends on rain, and sets before them a blessing and a curse to be proclaimed on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.
11.lookfor: Notice how the land itself teaches dependence on God, the repeated command to keep his words on heart and hand, and the two mountains at the end.

names.name: Dathan
names.gloss: A Reubenite who rebelled against Moses and was swallowed by the earth.

names.name: Abiram
names.gloss: Dathan's brother and partner in the rebellion.

names.name: Mount Gerizim
names.gloss: A mountain beside Shechem in central Canaan, where the blessing was to be spoken.

names.name: Mount Ebal
names.gloss: The mountain facing Gerizim across the valley of Shechem, where the curse was to be spoken.

names.name: oaks of Moreh
names.gloss: Sacred trees near Shechem where God first appeared to Abraham in Canaan.

insights.title: Watered by foot, or by rain
insights.body: In Egypt, Israel "watered it with your foot" (11:10), probably by opening and closing irrigation channels from the Nile with the foot. Canaan "drinks water from the rain of the sky" (11:11). A land without a great river teaches daily dependence on God, whose eyes are always on it (11:12).

insights.title: Former and latter rain
insights.body: God promises "the former rain and the latter rain" (11:14): the autumn rains that soften the ground for sowing, and the spring rains that fill out the grain. James pictures the farmer waiting patiently for both. If Israel turns to other gods, God will "shut up the sky" (11:17).

insights.title: The second paragraph of the Shema
insights.body: Verses 13 to 21 form the second paragraph of the Shema, recited by Jews morning and evening after the words of chapter 6. They repeat the commands to bind God's words on hand and forehead and write them on the doorposts (11:18-20), now linked with rain and harvest.

insights.title: Your eyes have seen
insights.body: Moses says he is not speaking to children who did not see God's great acts (11:2), but to "your eyes" that saw them (11:7). Among the acts he lists is the earth swallowing Dathan and Abiram (11:6). The witnesses of God's judgment are now the ones who must choose.

insights.title: Wherever your foot treads
insights.body: "Every place on which the sole of your foot treads shall be yours" (11:24). God repeats the promise almost word for word to Joshua as Israel prepares to cross.

insights.title: Two mountains
insights.body: Moses sets before them "a blessing and a curse" (11:26), to be proclaimed from Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal near Shechem (11:29). Chapter 27 gives the instructions and Joshua 8 carries them out. Centuries later the Samaritans built their temple on Gerizim, the mountain the woman at the well points to.

insights.title: A land that teaches
insights.body: A land that depends on rain kept Israel looking up. What in your circumstances keeps you aware that you depend on God?

12.summary: Israel must destroy the Canaanite shrines and bring their offerings only to the one place God will choose, though they may slaughter and eat meat at home as long as they do not eat the blood.
12.lookfor: Notice the repeated phrase "the place which Yahweh your God shall choose," who is invited to rejoice there, and the rules for eating meat away from it.

insights.title: The place he will choose
insights.body: Offerings must be brought "to the place which Yahweh your God shall choose... to put his name there" (12:5). The place is never named. Israel's sanctuary was at Shiloh for a time, and later Jerusalem was understood as the chosen place; King Josiah's reform closed the local shrines on the basis of this law.

insights.title: Right in his own eyes
insights.body: In the wilderness everyone did "whatever is right in his own eyes" (12:8). The same phrase ends the book of Judges, describing a nation that never settled down to this kind of worship. Deuteronomy links rest in the land with a single, ordered place of worship (12:10-11).

insights.title: Meat at home
insights.body: Before this, slaughtering an animal was close to a sacrifice. Now, since the sanctuary may be far away, Israel may kill and eat meat "within all your gates" (12:15), like game such as gazelle and deer. Ordinary meals are separated from offerings brought to the altar.

insights.title: The blood is the life
insights.body: Even at home, "don't eat the blood; for the blood is the life" (12:23); it must be poured out like water (12:24). Leviticus explains that God gave blood for atonement. The early church asked Gentile believers to abstain from blood.

insights.title: Rejoice together
insights.body: Worship at the chosen place is a feast: "you shall rejoice before Yahweh your God" (12:12), with sons and daughters, servants and the Levite. Deuteronomy repeatedly turns worship into a shared meal where the landless and the servants eat too (12:18).

insights.title: Sons and daughters in the fire
insights.body: The Canaanites "even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods" (12:31). Child sacrifice later appeared in Judah itself, at Topheth in the valley of Hinnom. Jeremiah says it was something God never commanded and never even thought of.

insights.title: How do they serve their gods?
insights.body: Israel must not ask, "How do these nations serve their gods? I will do likewise" (12:30). Where might you be borrowing the habits of your culture without asking whether they honour God?

13.summary: Anyone who entices Israel to serve other gods, whether a prophet with signs, a family member or a whole town, must be put to death.
13.lookfor: Notice that a sign coming true is not enough to trust a prophet, how close the enticer may be, and the call to investigate carefully before acting.

insights.title: Signs are not enough
insights.body: A prophet may give "a sign or a wonder" that comes true (13:1-2), but if his message is to follow other gods, Israel must not listen. The test is the message, not the miracle. Jesus warned that false prophets would show great signs, and Paul says even an angel preaching another gospel should not be believed.

insights.title: God is testing you
insights.body: Such a prophet is allowed because "Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart" (13:3). The test of loyalty echoes the Shema's call to love God with all the heart and soul.

insights.title: Your friend as your own soul
insights.body: The enticer might be a brother, a son or daughter, "the wife of your bosom, or your friend, who is as your own soul" (13:6). Loyalty to God comes before the closest human ties. Jesus speaks in a similar way about loving family more than him.

insights.title: Like a treaty's loyalty oath
insights.body: Ancient treaties, such as the Assyrian king Esarhaddon's succession treaty of 672 BC, required subjects to report anyone, even family members, who spoke against the king. Scholars have noted close parallels with this chapter. Here the great king whose loyalty is guarded is Yahweh.

insights.title: Inquire diligently
insights.body: Before acting against a town, Israel must "inquire, and make search, and ask diligently" (13:14) to be sure the report is true. Rumour is not enough. Later Jewish tradition taught that the case of the condemned town never actually happened and never would.

insights.title: Remove the evil
insights.body: "So you shall remove the evil from among you" (13:5) is a formula repeated many times in Deuteronomy. Paul quotes it when telling the Corinthians to deal with sin within the church, applying it as expulsion from the community rather than death.

insights.title: Loyalty under pressure
insights.body: These laws are severe, written for a nation whose whole life depended on loyalty to God. What voices, even well-meaning ones, pull you away from wholehearted love for God?

14.summary: As God's children and a holy people, Israel must avoid pagan mourning rites, eat only clean animals, and set aside tithes to be eaten joyfully before God and shared with the needy.
14.lookfor: Notice the reason given at the start, the simple tests for clean animals, and how the tithe becomes a celebration and, every third year, a food bank.

skim.advice: Verses 4 to 20 list clean and unclean animals, birds and fish, much as Leviticus 11 does. Skim the lists and read the opening, the tests in verses 6 and 9, and the tithe laws closely.

insights.title: You are his children
insights.body: "You are the children of Yahweh your God. You shall not cut yourselves" for the dead (14:1). Cutting the body and shaving the forehead were mourning rites of the surrounding peoples. The prophets of Baal cut themselves on Mount Carmel.

insights.title: Clean and unclean
insights.body: The rules for animals (14:6), fish with fins and scales (14:9) and birds follow Leviticus 11 closely. Mark comments that Jesus' teaching on what defiles made "all foods" clean, and Christian traditions have generally seen these laws as fulfilled.

insights.title: A kid in its mother's milk
insights.body: "You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk" (14:21) appears for the third time in the Torah. Jewish tradition built on it the separation of meat and dairy in kosher practice. Why it was given is unclear; suggestions include a pagan rite or simple respect for life.

insights.title: For the foreigner
insights.body: An animal that died naturally may not be eaten by Israel but may be given to the resident foreigner or sold (14:21). The holiness rules are for the covenant people, not imposed on everyone. Leviticus treats the matter differently, requiring washing for anyone who eats it.

insights.title: A tithe to enjoy
insights.body: The tithe is to be eaten "before Yahweh your God" at the chosen place (14:23). If the journey is too long, it can be turned into money and spent on "whatever your soul desires" there, including wine (14:26). Giving to God becomes a family feast of thanksgiving.

insights.title: Every third year
insights.body: Every third year the tithe is stored locally so the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow "shall come, and shall eat and be satisfied" (14:29). Worship and welfare are joined. Chapter 26 gives the prayer said when it is done.

insights.title: Eat and rejoice
insights.body: The tithe was not only given away but eaten in celebration before God. How might your giving become a source of joy rather than only duty?

15.summary: Every seventh year debts between Israelites are cancelled, the poor are to be lent to generously, Hebrew slaves are freed with gifts, and firstborn animals belong to God.
15.lookfor: Notice the tension between "there shall be no poor" and "the poor will never cease," the warning about the year of release, and how a freed slave is sent off.

insights.title: Shemittah: release
insights.body: "At the end of every seven years, you shall cancel debts" (15:1). The Hebrew shemittah means a letting go, the same word used for letting the land lie fallow in Exodus. Jewish tradition still calls the seventh year the shemittah year.

insights.title: No poor, yet always poor
insights.body: Verse 4 says "there shall be no poor with you" if Israel obeys; verse 11 says "the poor will never cease out of the land." The first is the goal, the second the reality that makes generosity a permanent duty. Jesus echoes verse 11: "you always have the poor with you."

insights.title: The prosbul
insights.body: Moses foresaw people refusing loans as the seventh year drew near (15:9). By the 1st century BC this was happening, and the sage Hillel introduced the prosbul, a court document that kept loans collectable so the poor could still borrow. The law's goal, generosity, was protected by changing its mechanism.

insights.title: Not empty-handed
insights.body: A freed Hebrew servant must not go "empty" (15:13) but be given generously from flock, threshing floor and winepress. The reason is Israel's own story: "you were a slave in the land of Egypt" (15:15). Israel too left Egypt carrying gifts.

insights.title: An ear to the door
insights.body: A servant who chooses to stay has his ear pierced with an awl against the door (15:17), a public mark of lifelong attachment to the household. Exodus gives the same rite. A psalm says "You have opened my ears" of willing obedience.

insights.title: Women too
insights.body: Here a Hebrew woman sold into service is freed in the seventh year just like a man (15:12, 15:17). Exodus had a separate rule for a daughter sold as a servant. Deuteronomy's version treats men and women alike.

insights.title: An open hand
insights.body: "You shall surely open your hand to him" (15:8), and "your heart shall not be grieved when you give" (15:10). Is your generosity more limited by your means or by your heart?

16.summary: Israel is to keep Passover, the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of Tents at the place God chooses, rejoicing with the poor, and to appoint judges who do strict justice.
16.lookfor: Notice who is invited to each feast, what Israel must remember at each, and the shift to justice at the end.

insights.title: Passover moves to the sanctuary
insights.body: In Exodus the Passover lamb was killed at home by each family. Here it must be sacrificed "at the place which Yahweh your God shall choose" (16:5-6). When King Josiah centralised worship, he held a great Passover in Jerusalem "as it is written in this book of the covenant."

insights.title: The bread of affliction
insights.body: Unleavened bread is "the bread of affliction; for you came out of the land of Egypt in haste" (16:3). The Passover Haggadah opens its telling by lifting the matzah and calling it the bread of affliction. Eating it each year keeps the memory physical.

insights.title: Bashal: roast or boil?
insights.body: The World English Bible says "You shall roast and eat it" (16:7), but the Hebrew verb bashal usually means to boil or cook, while Exodus forbids boiling the Passover. Chronicles seems to combine the two: they "roasted the Passover with fire" and boiled the other offerings.

insights.title: The widow at the feast
insights.body: At the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of Tents Israel must rejoice with "the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow" (16:11, 16:14). The most vulnerable are named guests. Deuteronomy's festivals are celebrations that no one is shut out of.

insights.title: Not empty
insights.body: Three times a year the men must appear before God, and "they shall not appear before Yahweh empty" (16:16); each gives "as he is able" (16:17). Paul likewise teaches giving in proportion to what one has.

insights.title: Justice, justice
insights.body: "You shall follow that which is altogether just" (16:20) translates a Hebrew phrase that repeats the word for justice: tsedek tsedek. It is one of the most quoted lines in Jewish ethics. A bribe, the verse before warns, "blinds the eyes of the wise" (16:19).

insights.title: Altogether joyful
insights.body: Of the Feast of Tents God says, "you shall be altogether joyful" (16:15). Is joy a command you take seriously in your worship?

17.summary: Laws on blemished sacrifices, the trial of idolaters on two or three witnesses, a central court for hard cases, and limits on any future king, who must write and read a copy of the law.
17.lookfor: Notice the rules of evidence, where difficult cases go, and the three things a king must not multiply.

insights.title: Two or three witnesses
insights.body: "At the mouth of one witness he shall not be put to death" (17:6); two or three are required, and the witnesses must throw the first stone (17:7). Jesus applies the principle to church discipline, and Paul to his own dealings with Corinth.

insights.title: A court for hard cases
insights.body: Cases "too hard for you" go to the priests and the judge at the chosen place (17:8-9), and their verdict must be followed (17:11). Jewish tradition saw this as the basis for the authority of the Sanhedrin, the high court of later times.

insights.title: Like all the nations
insights.body: Moses foresees Israel saying, "I will set a king over me, like all the nations" (17:14). Centuries later the elders say almost those words to Samuel. The law does not forbid a king, but it limits him sharply.

insights.title: Horses, wives and gold
insights.body: The king must not multiply horses, wives, or silver and gold (17:16-17). Solomon did all three: chariots and horses from Egypt, seven hundred wives who "turned away his heart," and silver as common as stones.

insights.title: A copy of this law
insights.body: The king must write "a copy of this law" (17:18) and read it all his life. The Greek translation rendered the phrase deuteronomion, "second law," which became the book's English name. The ideal king is a student of Scripture.

insights.title: Not above his brothers
insights.body: The king reads the law "that his heart not be lifted up above his brothers" (17:20). In the ancient world kings were often seen as above the law; here he is one Israelite among others, under the same commands.

insights.title: Power and the word
insights.body: The king's safeguard was daily reading of God's law. What safeguards keep you humble when you have authority over others?

18.summary: The Levites' share of the offerings, a ban on divination and contact with the dead, and God's promise to raise up a prophet like Moses, with a test for false prophets.
18.lookfor: Notice the long list of forbidden practices, the reason God promises a prophet, and how to tell a true word from a false one.

names.name: Horeb
names.gloss: Mount Sinai, where the people asked not to hear God's voice directly.

insights.title: Portions for the priests
insights.body: The priests receive "the shoulder, the two cheeks, and the inner parts" of sacrificed animals (18:3), with first fruits and the first fleece (18:4). Having no land, "Yahweh is their inheritance" (18:2). A Levite who comes to the sanctuary from elsewhere shares equally (18:6-8).

insights.title: Ways of reading the future
insights.body: The list of banned practices (18:10-11) covers child sacrifice, reading omens, sorcery, spells and consulting the dead. Such methods were common across the ancient Near East. King Saul, who had expelled the mediums, later visited one at Endor.

insights.title: Tamim: whole-hearted
insights.body: "You shall be perfect with Yahweh your God" (18:13). The Hebrew tamim means whole, complete or blameless, the word God used to Abraham. Jesus' call to be perfect as the Father is perfect uses the same idea.

insights.title: A prophet like me
insights.body: "Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from among you, of your brothers, like me" (18:15). Deuteronomy's ending says no prophet like Moses had yet arisen. The crowds asked whether Jesus was "the prophet," and Peter applies this verse to him.

insights.title: Why a prophet?
insights.body: The promise answers the people's request at Horeb: "Let me not hear again Yahweh my God's voice" (18:16). God approves and provides a human messenger with "my words in his mouth" (18:18). Prophecy is God's merciful way of speaking to people who cannot bear his direct voice.

insights.title: Does it happen?
insights.body: If a prophet's word does not come true, "that is the thing which Yahweh has not spoken" (18:22). Jeremiah uses this test against Hananiah. Chapter 13 adds the other side: even a true prediction does not validate a call to other gods.

insights.title: Listening instead of divining
insights.body: Israel was to listen to God's prophet instead of trying to read the future. Where are you tempted to seek certainty about the future instead of listening to what God has already said?

19.summary: Three cities of refuge are to be set apart for those who kill accidentally, boundary stones must not be moved, and a false witness is to receive the punishment he sought for another.
19.lookfor: Notice the example of the axe head, the difference between accident and murder, and the rule for false witnesses.

insights.title: The flying axe head
insights.body: The law gives a concrete case: two men chopping wood, and "the head slips from the handle" and kills one of them (19:5). The survivor must flee to a city of refuge before the avenger, "while his heart is hot," catches him (19:6). Law here is taught through real-life examples.

insights.title: Preparing the way
insights.body: Israel must "prepare the way" to the cities (19:3). Jewish tradition says roads to them were kept in good repair, with signs at crossroads pointing to "Refuge." Joshua later names six cities.

insights.title: Three more cities
insights.body: If the land grows, three more cities are to be added (19:8-9), making six or even nine. Rabbinic interpreters noted that Israel's borders never reached that size, so the extra cities waited for the future.

insights.title: Boundary stones
insights.body: "You shall not remove your neighbor's landmark" (19:14). Boundary stones marked a family's inheritance; in Babylon some were carved with curses on anyone who moved them. Proverbs repeats the warning, often to protect the poor from land-grabbing.

insights.title: Paying back the false witness
insights.body: If a witness lies, "you shall do to him as he had thought to do to his brother" (19:19). False testimony carries the penalty it tried to impose. Two witnesses are required for any charge (19:15).

insights.title: Eye for eye
insights.body: "Life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth" (19:21) set a limit on punishment, matching it to the wrong done. Similar rules appear in Hammurabi's laws. Jesus quotes the principle and calls his followers to go further by not retaliating.

insights.title: Room for accidents
insights.body: The law protects people who cause harm without intending it. How do you treat someone whose mistake hurt you but who meant no harm?

20.summary: Rules for war: priests encourage the army, certain men are sent home, distant cities are offered peace, the nearby Canaanite cities are to be destroyed, and fruit trees are spared in a siege.
20.lookfor: Notice who is excused from fighting, the difference between far and near cities, and the question about trees.

insights.title: Sent home from war
insights.body: A man with a new house, a new vineyard or a fiancée goes home, "lest he die in the battle" and another enjoy it (20:5-7). So does anyone afraid, "lest his brother's heart melt" (20:8). Gideon later sends home the fearful and is left with a small army.

insights.title: Excuses in a parable
insights.body: In Jesus' parable of the great banquet, guests excuse themselves because of a field, oxen and a new wife. Many scholars hear an echo of these exemptions: what excused a man from war is no excuse for refusing God's feast.

insights.title: The priest speaks first
insights.body: Before battle the priest says, "Don't let your heart faint!... for Yahweh your God is he who goes with you, to fight for you" (20:3-4). Israel's confidence rests not on numbers or chariots but on God's presence.

insights.title: Peace first
insights.body: Approaching a distant city, Israel must "proclaim peace to it" first (20:10); if it accepts, its people become forced labourers. Only if it refuses is it attacked. The Gibeonites later exploit this rule by pretending to come from far away.

insights.title: Nothing that breathes
insights.body: For the cities of Canaan, "you shall save alive nothing that breathes" (20:16), and the reason given is that they would teach Israel their practices (20:18). This is among the Bible's most troubling commands. Scholars debate its rhetoric, and Joshua and Judges show many Canaanites surviving and some, like Rahab, joining Israel.

insights.title: Is the tree a man?
insights.body: During a siege Israel must not cut down fruit trees: "is the tree of the field man, that it should be besieged by you?" (20:19). Assyrian reliefs show armies felling orchards. Jewish tradition drew from this verse a wider principle against needless destruction, called bal tashchit.

insights.title: Limits even in war
insights.body: Even in war, the law protects trees, newlyweds and the fearful. What limits should still hold for you when you are in conflict?

21.summary: Laws for an unsolved murder, a captive woman taken as wife, the firstborn of an unloved wife, a rebellious son, and the burial of an executed man hung on a tree.
21.lookfor: Notice how a whole town takes responsibility for an unknown killer, the limits placed on a husband and a father, and the rule about a body on a tree.

insights.title: Blood with no culprit
insights.body: When a body is found and the killer is unknown, the elders of the nearest town break a heifer's neck in an untilled valley and wash their hands, saying, "Our hands have not shed this blood" (21:7). Bloodshed defiles the land even when no one can be blamed. Pilate's handwashing at Jesus' trial recalls the gesture, but without its honesty.

insights.title: The captive wife
insights.body: A soldier may marry a captive woman, but only after she has mourned her parents for a full month (21:13). If he later rejects her, she goes free and may not be sold, "because you have humbled her" (21:14). The law accepts the harsh practice of its time while limiting the man's power over her.

insights.title: The loved and the unloved
insights.body: A man with two wives, "the one beloved, and the other hated," must not pass over the unloved wife's firstborn (21:15-16). Jacob's family, with Rachel loved more than Leah, is the obvious example. Chronicles explains how Reuben, Leah's firstborn, lost his birthright for another reason.

insights.title: A double portion
insights.body: The firstborn receives "a double portion of all that he has" (21:17), in Hebrew pi shenayim, literally "a mouth of two." When Elisha asks Elijah for a double portion of his spirit, he uses the same phrase, asking to be treated as Elijah's firstborn and heir.

insights.title: The rebellious son
insights.body: A son who is "stubborn and rebellious... a glutton and a drunkard" (21:20) may be brought by both parents to the elders and stoned. Jewish tradition hedged this law with so many conditions that the Talmud says it never actually happened. Jesus' critics called him "a gluttonous man and a drunkard," perhaps echoing this verse.

insights.title: Cursed on a tree
insights.body: An executed criminal's body hung on a tree must be buried the same day, "for he who is hanged is accursed of God" (21:23). John notes the authorities did not want the bodies left on crosses over the Sabbath. Paul writes that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse, quoting this verse.

insights.title: Shared responsibility
insights.body: A whole town had to answer for a death none of them caused. Where might you share responsibility for wrongs in your community that you did not personally commit?

22.summary: Laws on returning a neighbour's lost animals, clothing, sparing a mother bird, building a roof railing, avoiding mixtures, wearing fringes, and a series of laws on marriage and sexual wrongs.
22.lookfor: Notice how many laws are about care for others' property and safety, the small kindnesses required, and how the sexual laws distinguish victim from offender.

insights.title: You may not hide yourself
insights.body: If you see a neighbour's ox or sheep straying, you must bring it back; "You may not hide yourself" (22:3). Looking away is forbidden. Exodus applies the same rule even to an enemy's animal.

insights.title: The mother bird
insights.body: Taking eggs or chicks from a nest is allowed, but the mother must be let go, "that it may be well with you, and that you may prolong your days" (22:7). The promise is the same as for honouring parents. Rabbis noted that one of the easiest commands and one of the hardest carry the same reward.

insights.title: A railing on the roof
insights.body: Houses had flat roofs used for working, sleeping and praying, so a new house needed a railing "so that you don't bring blood on your house if anyone falls" (22:8). Peter prayed on a housetop, and David walked on his. This is an ancient building-safety law.

insights.title: Not mixing kinds
insights.body: Israel must not sow two kinds of seed in a vineyard, plough with an ox and a donkey together, or wear wool and linen woven together (22:9-11). Leviticus gives similar rules. Paul's warning not to be "unequally yoked" draws on the picture of mismatched animals.

insights.title: Fringes on four corners
insights.body: "You shall make yourselves fringes on the four corners of your cloak" (22:12). Numbers explains that the fringes remind Israel of God's commands. Observant Jews still wear them on the corners of the prayer shawl.

insights.title: Hard laws on marriage
insights.body: The laws in 22:13-29 reflect a society where a bride's virginity was a family matter and women had little legal standing. Some protect women: a husband who slanders his bride is fined and may never divorce her (22:19), and a woman attacked in the field is not punished, "for... there was no one to save her" (22:27). Others, like the death penalty in 22:21, are deeply troubling to modern readers.

insights.title: Care in small things
insights.body: Lost animals, bird nests and roof railings all receive God's attention in this chapter. What small, practical acts of care for others does your faith call you to?

23.summary: Laws on who may enter the assembly, keeping the war camp clean, sheltering runaway slaves, interest, vows, and eating from a neighbour's field.
23.lookfor: Notice who is excluded from the assembly and who is welcomed, the surprising rule about escaped slaves, and what a hungry traveller may take.

names.name: Balaam
names.gloss: The seer Moab hired to curse Israel, whose curses God turned into blessing.

names.name: Pethor
names.gloss: Balaam's home town near the Euphrates.

insights.title: Excluded and welcomed
insights.body: Eunuchs, Ammonites and Moabites are barred from the assembly (23:1-3). Nehemiah enforced the rule after the exile. Yet Ruth the Moabite becomes David's great-grandmother, and Isaiah promises eunuchs who keep God's covenant a place in his house better than sons and daughters.

insights.title: Your brother the Edomite
insights.body: "You shall not abhor an Edomite; for he is your brother. You shall not abhor an Egyptian, because you lived as a foreigner in his land" (23:7). Even the land of slavery is remembered for having once given Israel a home. Their grandchildren may join the assembly (23:8).

insights.title: A trowel among the weapons
insights.body: Soldiers must carry a trowel and bury their waste outside the camp, "for Yahweh your God walks in the middle of your camp" (23:14). Holiness reaches down to sanitation. Practical hygiene and reverence go together.

insights.title: Don't send him back
insights.body: "You shall not deliver to his master a servant who has escaped" (23:15); he may live wherever he chooses (23:16). Other ancient law codes, such as Hammurabi's, punished anyone who sheltered a runaway slave. Israel, once slaves themselves, were to be a refuge.

insights.title: No interest to a brother
insights.body: Israelites may not charge interest to one another on money or food (23:19), though they may to a foreigner in business (23:20). Loans to the poor were meant as help, not profit. The psalmist praises the one who "doesn't lend out his money for usury."

insights.title: Plucking grain
insights.body: A traveller may eat grapes or pluck ears of grain by hand in a neighbour's field but may not fill a container or use a sickle (23:24-25). When the disciples plucked grain, the Pharisees did not accuse them of theft, which this law allowed, but of working on the Sabbath.

insights.title: No need to vow
insights.body: "If you refrain from making a vow, it shall be no sin in you" (23:22), but a vow once made must be kept (23:23). Ecclesiastes says it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay.

insights.title: A place of refuge
insights.body: The runaway slave could live "where it pleases him best" (23:16). What would it mean for your community to be a place of safety for those escaping harm?

24.summary: Laws on divorce and remarriage, a year off for newlyweds, fair treatment of borrowers and workers, individual responsibility for crimes, and leaving gleanings for the poor.
24.lookfor: Notice how many laws protect the poor and powerless, the repeated reminder of slavery in Egypt, and the time limits set by the sunset.

names.name: Miriam
names.gloss: Moses' sister, struck with a skin disease after criticising Moses.

insights.title: A bill of divorce
insights.body: This law assumes divorce with a written certificate and forbids remarrying a former wife after she has married another (24:1-4). Rabbis debated what "some unseemly thing" (24:1) allowed: the school of Shammai said only unfaithfulness, the school of Hillel almost anything. Jesus said Moses permitted divorce "because of the hardness of your hearts."

insights.title: A year to cheer his wife
insights.body: A newly married man is free from military service and other duties for one year, and "shall cheer his wife whom he has taken" (24:5). The law protects a new marriage by giving it time.

insights.title: Dignity for the borrower
insights.body: A lender must not take a millstone as a pledge, "for he takes a life" (24:6), nor enter the borrower's house to choose a pledge (24:10-11). A poor man's cloak must be returned by sunset so he can sleep in it (24:13). Debt is not to strip anyone of food, privacy or warmth.

insights.title: Wages before sunset
insights.body: A poor hired worker must be paid the same day, "neither shall the sun go down on it" (24:15), whether Israelite or foreigner (24:14). James warns the rich that withheld wages cry out to the Lord.

insights.title: Each for his own sin
insights.body: "Every man shall be put to death for his own sin" (24:16), not for his parents' or children's. King Amaziah spared the sons of his father's assassins because of this law, and Ezekiel builds a whole chapter on the principle.

insights.title: The forgotten sheaf
insights.body: A sheaf forgotten in the field, the olives left on the tree and the grapes left on the vine are "for the foreigner, for the fatherless, and for the widow" (24:19-21). Ruth, a widowed foreigner, survived by gleaning in Boaz's field.

insights.title: Because you were slaves
insights.body: Twice the chapter grounds its commands in memory: "you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt" (24:18, 24:22). Israel's own experience of oppression is meant to shape how they treat the vulnerable.

insights.title: Before the sun goes down
insights.body: The poor worker "sets his heart on" his wages (24:15). Is there anything you owe someone that you are letting wait?

25.summary: Laws on limiting floggings, not muzzling a working ox, a brother's duty to his dead brother's widow, honest weights, and remembering what Amalek did.
25.lookfor: Notice the concern for the dignity of the punished, the ceremony of the sandal, and the command to remember and blot out Amalek.

names.name: Amalek
names.gloss: A desert people who attacked the weakest of Israel after the exodus.

insights.title: Forty stripes
insights.body: A flogging may not exceed forty strokes, "lest... your brother will be degraded in your sight" (25:3). The guilty man remains a brother. Later Jewish practice stopped at thirty-nine to avoid miscounting, and Paul says five times he received "forty stripes minus one."

insights.title: The ox that treads the grain
insights.body: "You shall not muzzle the ox when he treads out the grain" (25:4); the animal may eat as it works. Paul twice applies the verse to those who preach the gospel, arguing that workers deserve their pay.

insights.title: The brother-in-law's duty
insights.body: If a man dies childless, his brother should marry the widow so that a son can carry on the dead man's name (25:5-6). If he refuses, the widow pulls off his sandal and spits in his face before the elders (25:9). Jewish law still performs this release ceremony, called chalitzah.

insights.title: A hard penalty
insights.body: A woman who seizes a man's genitals to rescue her husband in a fight is to lose her hand (25:11-12). It is the only bodily mutilation prescribed in the Torah outside the principle of eye for eye. Rabbinic interpreters read it as requiring a monetary fine for the humiliation.

insights.title: Honest weights
insights.body: Merchants must not keep "diverse weights, one heavy and one light" (25:13), one for buying and one for selling. Proverbs calls a false balance an abomination, and Amos condemns traders who make the measure small. Stone shekel weights have been found in excavations across Israel.

insights.title: Remember Amalek
insights.body: Amalek attacked "all who were feeble behind you, when you were faint and weary" (25:18), preying on the stragglers. Israel must "blot out the memory of Amalek" and "not forget" (25:19). Jews read this passage on the Sabbath before Purim, since Haman is called an Agagite, linked to the Amalekite king.

insights.title: The ones at the back
insights.body: Amalek's crime was attacking the weak at the back of the line. Who are the stragglers in your community, and who is protecting them?

26.summary: When Israel enters the land, each family is to bring first fruits with a confession of God's saving acts, and declare before God that the third-year tithe has been given to the needy.
26.lookfor: Notice the words the worshipper speaks, the move from "he" to "us" in the confession, and the two declarations at the end.

insights.title: A wandering Aramean
insights.body: "My father was a Syrian ready to perish" (26:5) refers to Jacob, whose family came from Aram. The Hebrew can be read as a wandering or a perishing Aramean. The Passover Haggadah reads it differently again, as an Aramean, Laban, trying to destroy my father, and builds its retelling of the exodus on these verses.

insights.title: A short creed
insights.body: The worshipper recites Israel's story in four verses: ancestors few in number, oppression in Egypt, God's rescue, and the gift of the land (26:5-9). The scholar Gerhard von Rad called it a short historical creed. Faith is confessed as a story of what God has done.

insights.title: He, then us
insights.body: The confession begins in the third person, "My father... He went down into Egypt" (26:5), then switches: "The Egyptians mistreated us" (26:6). Each generation must tell the exodus as its own story.

insights.title: The first-fruits basket
insights.body: The farmer places the first fruits in a basket and the priest sets it before the altar (26:2, 26:4). The Mishnah describes villagers travelling to Jerusalem in procession with an ox crowned with olive leaves and a flute playing. The harvest gift becomes a public celebration.

insights.title: Not for the dead
insights.body: The farmer declares that none of the tithe was eaten in mourning, handled while unclean, or "given of it for the dead" (26:14). Offerings of food to dead ancestors were common in the region. Israel's gifts were to go to the living poor instead.

insights.title: You declared, he declared
insights.body: "You have declared today that Yahweh is your God" (26:17), and "Yahweh has declared today that you are a people for his own possession" (26:18). The covenant is spoken from both sides, the same pairing found throughout Scripture: I will be your God, and you will be my people.

insights.title: Telling your story
insights.body: Each Israelite had to tell how God brought them to where they stood. How would you tell the story of what God has done that brought you to today?

27.summary: Moses commands Israel to write the law on plastered stones and build an altar on Mount Ebal after crossing the Jordan, and to answer "Amen" to twelve curses pronounced by the Levites.
27.lookfor: Notice where the stones and altar go, how the tribes are divided between the two mountains, and the kinds of sins the curses name.

names.name: Mount Ebal
names.gloss: The mountain north of Shechem where the law was to be written and the curse spoken.

names.name: Mount Gerizim
names.gloss: The mountain south of Shechem where the blessing was to be spoken.

insights.title: Writing on plaster
insights.body: Large stones are to be coated with plaster and "all the words of this law" written on them "very plainly" (27:2, 27:8). Writing in ink on plaster was used in the ancient world for public texts; the Balaam inscription at Deir Alla was written that way. The law was to be posted where everyone could see it.

insights.title: Ebal or Gerizim?
insights.body: The altar is to be built on Mount Ebal (27:4), the mountain of the curse. The Samaritan version of the Torah reads Gerizim here, the mountain where the Samaritans later built their temple. The difference became part of a long dispute between Jews and Samaritans.

insights.title: Uncut stones
insights.body: The altar must be made of whole stones with no iron tool used on them (27:5-6), as Exodus also requires. God's altar was not to be shaped by human craft.

insights.title: Fulfilled by Joshua
insights.body: Joshua carries out this command after the victory at Ai, building the altar on Ebal, writing the law on stones, and reading the blessings and curses with the people on both mountains. Moses' instructions shape Israel's first act of worship west of the Jordan.

insights.title: Split between mountains
insights.body: Six tribes stand on Gerizim to bless and six on Ebal for the curse (27:12-13). Those on Gerizim are all sons of Jacob's wives Leah and Rachel; those on Ebal include all four sons of the servant wives, plus Reuben and Zebulun.

insights.title: Sins done in secret
insights.body: The twelve curses fall on things often done out of sight: an idol set up "in secret" (27:15), moving a boundary stone, misleading the blind, killing a neighbour "secretly" (27:24). The people answer "Amen" to each. Paul quotes the last curse to show that no one keeps the whole law.

insights.title: Saying Amen
insights.body: The whole nation had to say "Amen" to curses on itself if it broke the covenant. What are you agreeing to when you say Amen?

28.summary: Moses sets out the blessings that will follow obedience and the far longer list of curses that will follow disobedience, ending in siege, exile and a return to slavery in Egypt.
28.lookfor: Compare the length of the blessings with the curses, notice how the curses reverse the blessings, and watch the curses build toward exile.

skim.advice: The curses run on at length and grow more terrible. Read the blessings (verses 1 to 14) and the turn at verse 15 closely, then skim, pausing at verses 47 to 48 and the ending.

insights.title: Fourteen and fifty-four
insights.body: The blessings take fourteen verses; the curses take fifty-four. Many of the curses simply reverse a blessing: cursed in the city and the field, the basket and the kneading trough (28:16-17). The imbalance shows how seriously Moses takes the danger.

insights.title: Bronze sky, iron earth
insights.body: "Your sky that is over your head will be brass, and the earth that is under you will be iron" (28:23). An Assyrian loyalty treaty of 672 BC contains an almost identical curse, and scholars have noted many parallels between that treaty and this chapter.

insights.title: The head, not the tail
insights.body: Obedience will make Israel "the head, and not the tail" (28:13), lending and not borrowing. Disobedience reverses it: the foreigner "will be the head, and you will be the tail" (28:44).

insights.title: Without joy
insights.body: The curses come "because you didn't serve Yahweh your God with joyfulness, and with gladness of heart, by reason of the abundance of all things" (28:47). Ingratitude in plenty leads to slavery in want (28:48).

insights.title: Exile foretold
insights.body: A nation "from far... as the eagle flies; a nation whose language you will not understand" (28:49) will besiege Israel's cities and scatter the people (28:64). Readers have seen the Assyrian and Babylonian conquests in these words; Habakkuk describes the Babylonians flying like an eagle.

insights.title: The worst of sieges
insights.body: The chapter foresees parents eating their own children in siege (28:53-57). The books of Kings and Lamentations record that it happened, in Samaria and in Jerusalem. The Bible does not hide the horror of the covenant broken.

insights.title: Back to Egypt
insights.body: The final curse undoes the exodus: Israel will be brought "into Egypt again with ships" and sell themselves as slaves, "and nobody will buy you" (28:68). The rescue that began the nation's story is reversed.

insights.title: I wish it were evening
insights.body: "In the morning you will say, 'I wish it were evening!' and at evening you will say, 'I wish it were morning!'" (28:67). What does this picture of constant dread say about life without God's peace?

29.summary: In the land of Moab Moses renews the covenant with everyone present and with future generations, warning of the ruin that will follow any who turn to other gods.
29.lookfor: Notice who is included in the covenant, the image of a poisonous root, and the closing line about what is secret and what is revealed.

names.name: Sodom
names.gloss: A city destroyed by fire in Abraham's day, a byword for judgment.

names.name: Admah
names.gloss: A city near Sodom destroyed with it.

names.name: Zeboiim
names.gloss: Another of the cities of the plain destroyed with Sodom.

insights.title: Eyes that did not see
insights.body: Israel has seen every sign, "But Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day" (29:4). Seeing miracles is not the same as understanding. Paul quotes the words in Romans.

insights.title: Everyone stands here
insights.body: The covenant includes leaders, men, children, wives and foreigners, "from the one who cuts your wood to the one who draws your water" (29:10-11). The lowest workers stand alongside the elders. The Gibeonites later become woodcutters and water carriers for Israel.

insights.title: Those not here today
insights.body: Moses makes the covenant "with those who stand here with us today... and also with those who are not here with us today" (29:15). Jewish tradition understood this to include every future generation, as if all were present.

insights.title: A bitter root
insights.body: Moses warns against "a root that produces bitter poison" (29:18), a person who quietly turns from God while assuring himself, "I shall have peace" (29:19). Hebrews warns believers against a "root of bitterness" springing up and defiling many.

insights.title: Like Sodom and Admah
insights.body: A ruined land will look "like the overthrow of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim" (29:23). Hosea later hears God ask, "How can I make you like Admah?" as his compassion overrules his anger.

insights.title: Dots over the words
insights.body: "The secret things belong to Yahweh our God; but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children" (29:29). In Hebrew scrolls the words "to us and to our children" carry unusual dots above the letters, a scribal mark whose meaning is still debated. The verse has long been used to set limits on speculation about what God has not revealed.

insights.title: What is revealed
insights.body: God keeps some things hidden but gives what is revealed "that we may do all the words of this law" (29:29). Are you more drawn to what God has hidden or to what he has clearly said?

30.summary: Moses promises that if Israel returns to God from exile, God will gather them and circumcise their hearts, and he sets before them life and death, urging them to choose life.
30.lookfor: Count the times the word "return" appears, notice what God promises to do to their hearts, and listen for how near the command is said to be.

insights.title: Shuv: return
insights.body: The verb shuv, to turn or return, runs through the chapter: Israel will return to God (30:2), God will return and gather them (30:3), and will again rejoice over them (30:9). From the same root comes teshuvah, the Jewish word for repentance. Repentance is a homecoming on both sides.

insights.title: God will circumcise your heart
insights.body: In chapter 10 Israel was told to circumcise their own hearts. Here God promises, "Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart" (30:6). Jeremiah and Ezekiel later speak of God writing his law on hearts and giving a new heart.

insights.title: Not in heaven
insights.body: The command "is not in heaven" nor "beyond the sea" but "very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart" (30:12-14). Paul applies these words to the message of faith in Christ. A famous Talmudic story has rabbis quote "It is not in heaven" to insist the law is now entrusted to human interpreters.

insights.title: Gathered from the ends of heaven
insights.body: Even if Israel's outcasts are "in the uttermost parts of the heavens," God will gather them (30:4). After the exile, Nehemiah prayed these promises back to God, and Jewish hope of return has drawn on them ever since.

insights.title: Choose life
insights.body: "I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse. Therefore choose life" (30:19). Heaven and earth are called as witnesses again. The choice is not abstract: loving God is life itself, "for he is your life" (30:20).

insights.title: Not too hard
insights.body: "This commandment... is not too hard for you or too distant" (30:11). After all the curses, Moses insists obedience is possible, because God has come near in his word. Jesus says his yoke is easy and his burden light.

insights.title: Very near
insights.body: The word is "in your mouth and in your heart" (30:14). What would change if you believed God's word is closer and more doable than you think?

31.summary: Moses, now 120, hands leadership to Joshua, writes down the law for public reading every seven years, and is told that Israel will turn away, so he must teach them a song as a witness.
31.lookfor: Notice the words of encouragement repeated to Joshua, who must hear the law read, and why a song is needed.

names.name: Joshua
names.gloss: Moses' assistant, son of Nun, now appointed to lead Israel into the land.

insights.title: A hundred and twenty years
insights.body: Moses is "one hundred twenty years old today" (31:2). Stephen divides his life into three forties: in Egypt, in Midian, and leading Israel. A traditional Jewish blessing still wishes people long life until a hundred and twenty.

insights.title: He will not forsake you
insights.body: "Be strong and courageous... He will not fail you nor forsake you" (31:6), said to all Israel and then to Joshua (31:7-8). God repeats the promise to Joshua, and Hebrews applies it to believers.

insights.title: Reading the law aloud
insights.body: Every seven years at the Feast of Tents the law is to be read to all Israel (31:10-11). Jewish tradition calls this gathering Hakhel, and the Mishnah records a king reading Deuteronomy to the people in the Temple. Ezra's public reading of the law in Nehemiah 8 took place in the seventh month.

insights.title: Men, women, children, foreigners
