insights.body: Everyone must assemble to hear: "the men and the women and the little ones, and the foreigners" (31:12), so that children who have not known may learn (31:13). The law was not only for priests and scholars.

insights.title: I will hide my face
insights.body: God tells Moses plainly that Israel will turn to other gods, and "I will hide my face from them" (31:17-18). Jewish thought calls this hester panim, the hiding of God's face, and has used it to speak of times when God seems absent.

insights.title: Why a song?
insights.body: Moses is to teach Israel a song that "will not be forgotten out of the mouths of their descendants" (31:21). Songs are remembered when laws are forgotten. When disaster comes, the song will testify that God warned them.

insights.title: Beside the ark
insights.body: The book of the law is placed "by the side of the ark" as a witness (31:26). Centuries later, a book of the law found in the Temple during King Josiah's repairs sparked a national reform.

insights.title: Leaving well
insights.body: Moses spends his last days preparing others to go on without him. What are you preparing to hand on?

32.summary: The Song of Moses calls heaven and earth to hear how Israel's faithful Rock cared for them, how they turned to other gods, how God will judge and then vindicate his people; then Moses is told to climb Mount Nebo to die.
32.lookfor: Watch for the name "Rock," the pictures of God as father and eagle, and the turn from judgment to mercy near the end.

names.name: Jeshurun
names.gloss: A poetic name for Israel, probably meaning "upright one."

names.name: Mount Nebo
names.gloss: A peak in the Abarim range in Moab, overlooking Jericho and the Jordan valley.

insights.title: The Rock
insights.body: God is called "the Rock" again and again (32:4, 32:15, 32:18, 32:30-31): solid, faithful, unchanging, unlike the false rocks other nations trust (32:37). Paul calls Christ the rock that followed Israel in the wilderness.

insights.title: The number of the sons of God
insights.body: The World English Bible says God set the boundaries of the peoples "according to the number of the children of Israel" (32:8). A Dead Sea Scroll copy and the Greek translation read "sons of God" instead, picturing the nations assigned to heavenly beings while Israel remains God's own portion (32:9). Many scholars think that was the original reading.

insights.title: Like an eagle
insights.body: God is like "an eagle that stirs up her nest" and carries her young on her wings (32:11). At Sinai God said he bore Israel "on eagles' wings." The picture combines care with pushing the young to fly.

insights.title: Jeshurun grew fat
insights.body: "But Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked" (32:15). Jeshurun is a fond name for Israel, probably from the word for upright; here it is ironic. Isaiah uses the name tenderly again.

insights.title: Paul's favourite song
insights.body: Paul quotes this song repeatedly: God provoking Israel to jealousy by "those who are not a people" (32:21), "Vengeance is mine" (32:35), and "Rejoice, you nations, with his people" (32:43), which Paul reads as including the Gentiles. Hebrews also quotes it.

insights.title: Sacrificed to demons
insights.body: Israel "sacrificed to demons, not God" (32:17). Paul uses the same reasoning when warning the Corinthians against meals offered to idols.

insights.title: Judgment, then compassion
insights.body: The song moves from Israel's ingratitude to God's judgment and then to mercy: "Yahweh will judge his people, and have compassion on his servants" (32:36). "I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal" (32:39). Revelation pictures the redeemed singing "the song of Moses" and of the Lamb.

insights.title: It is your life
insights.body: Moses says the law is "no vain thing for you; because it is your life" (32:47). What would it mean for God's word to be your life rather than an addition to it?

33.summary: Before his death Moses blesses the tribes of Israel one by one, framed by praise of God who came from Sinai and whose everlasting arms hold his people.
33.lookfor: Compare these blessings with Jacob's in Genesis 49, notice which tribe is missing, and listen to the opening and closing praise.

names.name: Seir
names.gloss: The mountains of Edom, from where God is pictured coming.

names.name: Mount Paran
names.gloss: Mountains in the desert south of Canaan, linked with God's coming.

names.name: Jeshurun
names.gloss: A poetic name for Israel, "the upright one."

insights.title: Two farewell blessings
insights.body: Jacob blessed his twelve sons before he died; now Moses blesses the tribes. Jacob had cursed the anger of Levi and Simeon; here Levi receives a long blessing as the priestly tribe (33:8-11), and Simeon is not mentioned at all.

insights.title: Where is Simeon?
insights.body: Simeon is missing from Moses' list. In Joshua, Simeon's land lies inside Judah's territory, and the tribe seems to have been absorbed into Judah. Its drop in numbers between the two censuses of Numbers may also be in view.

insights.title: Levi's hard loyalty
insights.body: Levi "said of his father, and of his mother, 'I have not seen him'" (33:9). This recalls the golden calf, when the Levites sided with God even against their own relatives. Their reward is to teach Israel the law and serve at the altar (33:10).

insights.title: Him who lived in the bush
insights.body: Joseph's blessing includes "the good will of him who lived in the bush" (33:16), a reference to the burning bush where God first spoke to Moses. At the end of his life Moses still names God by that first meeting.

insights.title: Between his shoulders
insights.body: Benjamin "dwells between his shoulders" (33:12), under God's protection. Jerusalem and its Temple stood on the border between Benjamin and Judah, and some interpreters read the line as pointing to God's house in Benjamin's territory.

insights.title: Treasures of the sand
insights.body: Zebulun and Issachar "draw out the abundance of the seas, the hidden treasures of the sand" (33:19). Their territory reached toward the Mediterranean coast near Acco, a region later famous for glassmaking from its sand and for dye from sea snails.

insights.title: Everlasting arms
insights.body: "The eternal God is your dwelling place. Underneath are the everlasting arms" (33:27). The blessings end not with the tribes but with the God who holds them, and a final cry: "You are happy, Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by Yahweh?" (33:29).

insights.title: Strength for your days
insights.body: Asher is promised, "As your days, so your strength will be" (33:25). What would it mean to trust God for strength one day at a time?

34.summary: Moses climbs Mount Nebo, sees the whole promised land, dies in Moab at 120 and is buried by God in an unknown grave; Joshua takes his place, but no prophet like Moses arises again.
34.lookfor: Notice how much of the land Moses sees, who buries him, and the closing praise of Moses.

names.name: Mount Nebo
names.gloss: A peak in Moab across the Jordan from Jericho; today's Mount Nebo in Jordan is the traditional site.

names.name: Pisgah
names.gloss: The ridge of which Nebo is the summit.

names.name: Zoar
names.gloss: A town at the southern end of the Dead Sea, spared in Lot's day.

names.name: Beth Peor
names.gloss: A place in Moab near which Moses was buried.

insights.title: Who wrote this chapter?
insights.body: Moses' own death is described in the past tense, along with the comment that "no man knows where his tomb is to this day" (34:6). The Talmud records two views: that Joshua wrote these last verses, or that Moses wrote them at God's dictation, in tears.

insights.title: Seeing it all
insights.body: From Nebo God shows Moses the land from Gilead to Dan, Naphtali, Ephraim, Manasseh, Judah to the western sea, the south and Jericho (34:1-3). From the real Mount Nebo one cannot see all of this, which suggests a God-given vision of the whole land. Moses sees the promise kept, though he cannot enter.

insights.title: Buried by God
insights.body: "He buried him" (34:6): the text implies God himself buried Moses, and the grave was never known. Jude refers to a tradition of the archangel Michael disputing with the devil over Moses' body.

insights.title: His eye was not dim
insights.body: "His eye was not dim, nor his strength gone" (34:7). Moses did not die of weakness but at God's word (34:5). Earlier he had said he could no longer go out and come in, probably meaning as Israel's leader rather than in body.

insights.title: Joshua takes up the work
insights.body: Joshua is "full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands on him" (34:9), and Israel listens to him. The handover commanded in Numbers is complete, and the next book opens, "After the death of Moses."

insights.title: No prophet like Moses
insights.body: "There has not arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom Yahweh knew face to face" (34:10). This looks back to God's promise of a prophet like Moses and leaves it open. The New Testament presents Jesus as that prophet, and at the transfiguration Moses appears with him on a mountain inside the land.

insights.title: Seeing but not entering
insights.body: Moses saw the land but died outside it. Hebrews says the faithful died "not having received the promises, but having seen them." How do you live faithfully toward promises you may not see fulfilled?

intro.who: Jewish and Christian tradition receive it as Moses' farewell speeches, with the account of his death added by another hand (the Talmud suggests Joshua). Many modern scholars link its core to the "book of the law" found in the Temple under King Josiah in 622 BC, expanded during the exile.
intro.when: It is set on the plains of Moab in the eleventh month of the fortieth year after the exodus, just before Israel crosses the Jordan (Deuteronomy 1:3). Proposed dates for its writing run from Moses' time to the 7th or 6th century BC.
intro.why: Moses calls a new generation to love Yahweh with all their heart and keep his covenant in the land, setting before them life and death, blessing and curse. Jesus quotes it more than any other book of the Torah.
